content: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) have issued updated guidelines on HIV and infant feeding, focusing on the duration of breastfeeding and the role of health services in supporting optimal feeding practices for mothers living with HIV. These guidelines emphasize the importance of exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, followed by continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods up to two years or beyond, while ensuring antiretroviral therapy for HIV-positive mothers to minimize transmission risks. Baker et al. (2016) analyzed global trends in the sales of commercial milk-based formulas, highlighting a significant shift in infant and young child feeding practices. This transition raises concerns about the potential impact on breastfeeding rates and child health outcomes. Hojšak et al. (2018) presented a position paper from the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) on young child formulas, discussing their nutritional role and appropriate use in the diets of children aged 1–3 years. Fewtrell et al. (2017) provided a comprehensive review on complementary feeding, emphasizing the timing, types, and methods of introducing solid foods to infants. The ESPGHAN Committee on Nutrition outlined evidence-based recommendations to support healthy growth and development. Walther et al. (2022) compared the nutritional composition of plant-based drinks and cow’s milk, noting significant differences in protein, calcium, and other essential nutrients. The study cautioned against using plant-based drinks as direct substitutes for cow’s milk in young children without proper fortification. Pérez-Escamilla et al. (2019) debated whether exclusive breastfeeding for six months remains the optimal recommendation, considering emerging evidence on infant nutrition and health outcomes. The authors reaffirmed the benefits of exclusive breastfeeding while acknowledging the need for context-specific guidance. Kramer and Kakuma (2012) conducted a Cochrane review on the optimal duration of exclusive breastfeeding, concluding that six months of exclusive breastfeeding provides significant health benefits for both infants and mothers. Greer et al. (2019) examined the effects of early nutritional interventions, including maternal dietary restrictions, breastfeeding, hydrolyzed formulas, and the timing of allergenic food introduction, on the development of atopic diseases in children. Chaparro et al. (2006) investigated the timing of umbilical cord clamping and its impact on iron status in Mexican infants. Delayed cord clamping was associated with improved iron stores, reducing the risk of anemia in early infancy. Meinzen-Derr et al. (2006) identified a link between exclusive breastfeeding, maternal anemia, and the risk of infant anemia in a Mexican cohort. The findings underscore the importance of maternal nutrition in preventing anemia during infancy. The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) published a report advocating for improved infant and young child feeding practices globally, emphasizing the critical role of breastfeeding in the first hour of life and beyond. Iannotti et al. (2014) highlighted the potential of eggs as a nutrient-dense food to improve maternal and child nutrition in low-income settings. The study called for increased access to eggs as part of sustainable nutrition strategies. Monteiro et al. (2019) discussed the health implications of ultra-processed foods using the NOVA classification system. The study linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods to poor diet quality and adverse health outcomes. Pries et al. (2017) examined the consumption of commercially produced snack foods and sugar-sweetened beverages during the complementary feeding period in urban contexts across Africa and Asia. The findings raised concerns about the nutritional quality of these foods and their impact on child health. Keats et al. (2021) reviewed effective interventions to address maternal and child malnutrition, highlighting the importance of integrated approaches that combine nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive strategies. Dewey et al. (2022) demonstrated that small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements significantly reduce severe wasting and stunting among young children. The meta-analysis provided robust evidence supporting the use of these supplements in vulnerable populations. The WHO guideline development group, comprising experts from various fields, collaborated to produce evidence-based recommendations on complementary feeding for infants and young children aged 6–23 months. The guidelines aim to improve child nutrition and health outcomes globally.
